# DevFn

> Trusted local profiles, process and Compose lifecycle, port leases, readiness, and localhost routes.

This file concatenates the full text of every documentation page so it can be loaded into
an LLM-based assistant in a single shot. For a page index, see /docs/llms.txt.

# Documentation

<!-- page:docs:configuration.md path:/docs/configuration -->
# Configuration

> Declare project identity, ports, processes, Compose services, and profiles.


DevFn discovers `devfn.config.ts`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, or `.json` while walking upward. Each manifest has `version: 1`, a stable `project.id`, and named profiles. It may define ports, native processes, Compose services, hostname routes, prerequisites, environment outputs, and a repository-relative organization policy.

JavaScript-family manifests are executable but must be self-contained; imports and `require()` are rejected. JSON is parsed as data. Both forms require digest-bound trust before loading. Repository-relative paths reject absolute paths, `..` traversal, and symlink escape. References and dependency cycles are validated before lifecycle mutation.

A port can select exact, preferred, range, ephemeral, loopback/public, or contiguous-block allocation. Processes declare an adapter, command or script, dependencies, readiness, environment allowlist, and optional secret names. Compose services select a declared service, port mappings, health, and persistence. Profiles select these resources transitively and may enable the shared proxy. Hostname routes default to `.localhost`; a route can instead select a machine-registered development `domain`, a shared `host` label, and a `path` with prefix or exact matching.

Before startup, DevFn generates `DEVFN_PORT_<NAME>` for each selected port (plus its configured `env` alias) and `DEVFN_URL_<NAME>` for HTTP health ports and routed targets. Profile values, node values, process `command` arguments, package scripts, and command-health arguments can refer to these and other declared keys with `{{env.NAME}}`. Missing references and cycles fail before any lease, file, process, or service mutation. Arguments are passed as literal argv without a shell. Credentials must stay out of literals and argv: URL userinfo, credential headers, credential-named flags, form fields, and JSON keys are rejected, so pass secrets through `envAllowlist` and `secretEnv`.

Resources declare backends and data stores (`service`, `database`, `broker`, `cache`, `object-store`, `browser`) with local or credential-free remote targets. A profile selects each target independently of which code runs locally. DevFn validates the topology before mutation, emits `DEVFN_RESOURCE_*` endpoint and namespace values through the same templates, isolates namespaces per runtime unless sharing is explicit, and records a redacted plan with value provenance. See [resource targets and namespaces](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md#resource-targets-and-namespaces).

Read the [complete configuration reference](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md) for field shapes, adapter values, health check examples, [endpoint templates](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md#startup-endpoint-and-template-resolution), hostname and domain routing, and policy rules. Treat examples as a starting point and verify every process command before trusting a manifest.

---

<!-- page:docs:getting-started.md path:/docs/getting-started -->
# Getting started

> Initialize, trust, inspect, and start a local profile.


Install or invoke `@devfn/cli` from the repository you want to run. `init` previews detected configuration; review it before accepting generated files. The first load of any manifest needs `--trust`, even for JSON, because it can declare lifecycle commands. Trust is bound to the exact manifest digest, so an edit requires review and trust again.

```sh
npx @devfn/cli init
# Review the preview, then write the manifest:
npx @devfn/cli init --yes
npx @devfn/cli doctor --trust
npx @devfn/cli up --profile default
npx @devfn/cli status --json
npx @devfn/cli logs app
npx @devfn/cli down
```

Profiles containing public processes or ports also require `--allow-public` on every start. `up --json` emits one lifecycle receipt with state, instance and invocation IDs, allocations, managed resources, and resolved URLs. Read-only commands return structured command data in JSON mode; failures use stable `DEVFN_*` codes and exit nonzero. `devfn restart` checks the profile, registered domains, and replacement ports before stopping a ready instance, then starts it again from the current working tree; if that start fails, the previous processes are not relaunched.

Runtime files default to `.devfn/` with owner-only permissions. If the manifest configures `environmentOutputs`, inspect and back up any pre-existing target file before starting: DevFn overwrites configured outputs and cannot restore their former contents. See the [migration guide](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/migration.md).

---

<!-- page:docs:index.md path:/docs -->
# DevFn

> Trusted lifecycle orchestration for local development.


DevFn coordinates native application processes, Docker Compose infrastructure, machine-local port leases, readiness, logs, diagnostics, and stable `.localhost` or machine-registered development-domain URLs through one command contract. It identifies each worktree instance so concurrent local environments do not silently share mutable resources.

Start with [getting started](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/getting-started.md), then define a [manifest](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/configuration.md) and operate a [profile](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/lifecycle.md). Review [trust and exposure](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/security.md) before loading a manifest or opening a public port. Existing projects should follow the [migration guide](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/migration.md).

DevFn does not replace HostFn deployment, browser evidence, ExtFn extension semantics, Docker Compose, Wrangler, or Xcode. It coordinates local runtimes through explicit adapters. Version 0.1 uses CLI-managed state rather than a daemon.

---

<!-- page:docs:lifecycle.md path:/docs/lifecycle -->
# Lifecycle and diagnostics

> Start, inspect, stop, and recover one worktree instance.


`devfn up` plans resources in dependency order, reserves ports before mutation, starts selected native processes and Compose services, verifies readiness, registers proxy routes, and returns a machine-readable receipt. If an invocation fails, rollback targets resources created by that invocation. `status`, `logs`, and `doctor` expose live state and diagnostics; `down` stops only the exact worktree instance. `restart` validates the selected profile, registered domains, and replacement ports while the ready instance keeps running, then stops it and starts it again from the current working tree; a failed restart does not relaunch the previous processes. Status reports a ready instance as `degraded` when its declared startup inputs, Compose configuration, Caddy owner, or committed routes no longer match its receipt, and the next `up` replaces it.

There is no background daemon in version 0.1. Receipts, process logs, and generated runtime outputs live under the configured runtime directory (`.devfn/` by default). Configured `environmentOutputs[].path` files can live elsewhere within the repository. Machine-wide trust records, port registry, lifecycle locks, and proxy state instead use `$XDG_STATE_HOME/devfn`, falling back to `~/.local/state/devfn`. Account for both locations when inspecting or cleaning up state. Process ownership uses a PID birth signature where the host supplies one and judges each recorded process with its whole process group, so cleanup refuses a reused PID. When a live process's identity cannot be verified, teardown reports a cleanup error, leaves the receipt `degraded`, and keeps its leases and routes until a later `down` can verify or stop it. `devfn ports gc` reconciles leases and removes the routes of instances whose recorded owners are all verified dead, such as a deleted worktree.

Ordinary `down` does not delete persistent Docker volumes. It is also not a general reset command. Explicit configured environment outputs may have overwritten files that existed before adoption; inspect them before manual cleanup. The [core package](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/core.md), [process supervisor](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/processes.md), and [migration guide](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/migration.md) describe lifecycle boundaries.

---

<!-- page:docs:migration.md path:/docs/migration -->
# Migrating a project

> Adopt DevFn while preserving existing startup and data paths.


Preserve existing scripts and Compose data. Run `devfn init`, inspect confirmed and proposed detections, then edit the manifest until every command, dependency, port, profile, and health check is explicit. Run `devfn doctor --trust` and resolve prerequisites and exact-port collisions before the first start.

Back up any pre-existing path named by `environmentOutputs[].path`; DevFn overwrites configured outputs and does not restore previous contents. Inspect the resolved Compose configuration as well: DevFn derives the Compose project name from the project prefix and worktree owner, so a project-scoped named volume can resolve to a new, empty volume. Back up existing database contents before the first start. Start with a minimal profile, compare behavior against manual startup, then add full, OAuth, test, or docs profiles. Verify that `devfn down` preserves databases and volumes before making it the daily workflow.

To roll back, run `down`, inspect the configured runtime directory and output paths, and remove only DevFn-generated files that did not replace user content. Then remove the manifest and resume the preserved scripts. The [source migration guide](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/migration.md) gives the complete checklist.

---

<!-- page:docs:packages.md path:/docs/packages -->
# Packages

> Map DevFn's eight packages to their responsibilities.


| Package | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `@devfn/cli` | `devfn` command, initialization, diagnostics, lifecycle, and JSON receipts. |
| `@devfn/core` | Dependency plans, journals, receipts, rollback, and diagnostics. |
| `@devfn/config` | Manifest discovery, validation, digest trust, and policy. |
| `@devfn/ports` | Lock-protected machine port leases, reconciliation, and reports. |
| `@devfn/processes` | Native process supervision, logs, readiness, and ownership. |
| `@devfn/compose` | Worktree-scoped Docker Compose infrastructure. |
| `@devfn/proxy` | Shared Caddy route control for `.localhost` and registered development-domain names. |
| `@devfn/testing` | Deterministic fixtures and fake listeners. |

The packages expose separate public entry points. Use the CLI for the supported end-to-end workflow; lower-level packages are for integrations that preserve DevFn's identity, trust, and ownership contracts. Detailed source guides are under [reference](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/index.md).

---

<!-- page:docs:ports-and-proxy.md path:/docs/ports-and-proxy -->
# Ports and localhost routes

> Allocate per-worktree ports and publish concrete local URLs.


`@devfn/ports` uses machine-local locking and worktree identity to allocate and reconcile exact, preferred, ranged, ephemeral, and contiguous-block ports. `exact: true` fails closed on collision. Public port exposure needs an explicit manifest choice and `--allow-public` on each start. Inspect allocations with `devfn ports` and the full machine registry with `devfn ports report`.

`@devfn/proxy` manages one lock-protected Caddy route registry with concrete hostnames and loopback targets. It validates generated configuration before reload, returns 404 for unknown hosts, and refuses to take over an unrelated Caddy admin endpoint. Caddy listens on loopback only: ports 8080 and 8443 on macOS, which appear in published URLs, and 80 and 443 on Linux, which need `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` at or below 80 or `cap_net_bind_service` on the Caddy binary. A service already leasing a listener port must move to another port before a proxy route is activated.

Hostname templates accept `{project}` and `{instance}` and resolve to `.localhost` by default. Other development domains need explicit machine registration with `devfn domains register dev.example.test --tls internal`; the domain must already resolve only to loopback, and DevFn never edits DNS, hosts files, or trust stores. A registered route gets `<host>-<worktree>-<suffix>.<domain>` per worktree, plus `<host>.<domain>` for the primary worktree, and can match a path prefix or exact path, optionally stripping the prefix. Internal TLS uses Caddy's local CA, which clients must trust explicitly; certificate TLS uses PEM files whose DNS subject alternative names cover every generated hostname.

DevFn returns HTTP URLs only for explicit hostname routes or ports named by HTTP health checks. A database or arbitrary TCP listener remains a transport allocation rather than an invented HTTP URL. The [configuration reference](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md) covers port and hostname fields, while [ports](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/ports.md) and [proxy](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/proxy.md) document package behavior.

---

<!-- page:docs:processes-and-compose.md path:/docs/processes-and-compose -->
# Processes and Compose

> Run native applications and worktree-scoped infrastructure.


Native process adapters include `command`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `turbo`, `wrangler`, `xcode`, and `extfn`. Commands run locally under supervision with declared working directory, dependency order, environment, ports, readiness, and shutdown timeout. Turbo, Wrangler, and ExtFn resolve project-local binaries without downloading missing tools; pnpm follows the repository's Corepack pin. Yarn and Bun discovery is proposed and does not create guessed processes.

Compose services use Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer. DevFn names the Compose project with a digest of the project prefix and the worktree owner, generates host-port overrides with loopback mapping by default, starts only the requested service with `--no-deps`, and preserves persistent volumes during ordinary cleanup. Services with `secretEnv` disable Docker log persistence and cannot use log-pattern readiness. Sibling Compose services on a shared network receive container-context `DEVFN_URL_*` values such as `http://web:8080`, while native processes receive loopback URLs. Ready receipts fingerprint the effective Compose service and its referenced definitions, so an edited Compose source degrades status and the next start restarts the owned service.

Readiness checks may use HTTP, TCP, command, or log patterns. Local-process exposure verification needs `lsof` on macOS/Linux or `netstat` on Windows. Run `doctor` to surface missing prerequisites. See [processes](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/processes.md), [Compose](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/compose.md), and [configuration](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md) for exact settings.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/cli.md path:/docs/reference/cli -->
# @devfn/cli

> Source package guide for @devfn/cli.


DevFn runs heterogeneous local environments through one command contract while keeping application processes native and infrastructure Compose-backed where appropriate.

```bash
npx @devfn/cli init
npx @devfn/cli init --yes
npx @devfn/cli doctor --trust
npx @devfn/cli up --profile default
npx @devfn/cli status --json
npx @devfn/cli logs app
npx @devfn/cli down
npx @devfn/cli domains register dev.example.test --tls internal
npx @devfn/cli domains list
```

Registering a domain requires it to resolve already, and only to loopback addresses (`127.0.0.1`, or `::1` where available). A reserved name such as `dev.example.test` does not resolve until you configure local DNS for it yourself; DevFn never edits resolver, hosts or trust-store configuration.

Profiles that declare public processes or ports require `--allow-public` on every start.
`devfn ports gc` reconciles leases and retires listener claims with conclusive evidence. It removes the proxy routes of an instance only when its recorded process and container owners, including those of failed or interrupted starts, are all verified dead (for example a deleted worktree); an owner whose identity cannot be read counts as running. Finally, gc collects released records.
`devfn restart` validates the selected profile and registered domains, then reserves replacement ports before stopping a ready instance. A rejected domain, route, or port selection leaves that instance running. After those checks it stops the instance and starts it again from the current working tree. If that start fails, the previous processes are not relaunched and the error says so. Cleanup of the failed start can itself fail and leave some of its new processes or containers running; when the error reports cleanup errors, run `devfn down` again.

The first load of any manifest requires `--trust` because JSON and executable manifests can both declare lifecycle commands. Trust is bound to the manifest digest, so edits require review and trust again. Lifecycle mutations return receipts in JSON mode; read-only commands return command-specific structured data, and failures use stable error codes. Runtime files are written with restrictive permissions under `.devfn/` by default.

For automation, `devfn up --json` emits one lifecycle receipt object containing `state`, `instanceId`, `invocationId`, allocations, managed processes/services, and resolved URLs. Failures emit `{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "DEVFN_*", "message": "..." } }` and exit nonzero. Treat fields not documented here as additive.

DevFn v0.1 uses transactional CLI-managed state rather than a daemon. Runtime logic is platform-aware; macOS and Linux are the validated first-release hosts, while Windows process ownership is implemented but requires platform CI before it is declared supported.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/compose.md path:/docs/reference/compose -->
# @devfn/compose

> Source package guide for @devfn/compose.


Requires Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer. Starts only declared Compose services with `--no-deps` under a project name whose readable prefix is case folded and whose digest includes the exact prefix and opaque owner bytes; case-distinct prefixes remain separate even if their readable names normalize alike. It replaces source mappings with loopback or explicitly public DevFn host-port mappings while retaining conventional container ports, and never removes persistent volumes during ordinary cleanup. Secret-bearing services disable Docker log persistence.

Ready receipts fingerprint the selected effective Compose service, referenced volume/network/config/secret definitions, selected config-file contents, and noncredential environment values after Compose interpolation. Default and include-scoped env files participate when they affect that service; assignments with no effect and unrelated services do not. Ordered dotenv declarations preserve the value captured by an earlier assignment, while credential-derived config content is masked and an ordinary fallback remains part of the digest. Compose source references to inherited host variables such as `HOME` require an explicit `envAllowlist` entry, so ambient values do not silently enter a receipt. Credential-named and `secretEnv` values are excluded from the fingerprint; literal nonsecret fields retain their value even when the same bytes appear in a secret. Put credentials in `secretEnv`, not in Compose config files. Source graphs, alias expansion and local path interpolation are bounded before Compose reads them for endpoint planning. On Compose 2.24.4, a bounded source inventory supplies uninterpolated field provenance when its `--no-interpolate` option cannot open an interpolated `env_file` or bind-mount path.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/config.md path:/docs/reference/config -->
# @devfn/config

> Source package guide for @devfn/config.


Validated DevFn project manifests and organization port-policy contracts. Every manifest can declare lifecycle commands and must be reviewed and explicitly trusted before the DevFn CLI loads its exact digest; executable manifests additionally must be self-contained.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/configuration.md path:/docs/reference/configuration -->
# Configuration contract

> Manifest fields, ports, processes, services, profiles, and policy.


DevFn discovers `devfn.config.ts`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, or `.json` while walking upward from the current directory. JavaScript-family manifests are executable code, require digest-bound trust, and must be self-contained (no imports or `require()`). JSON is data-only.

## Top-level manifest

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `version: 1` | yes | Manifest schema version. |
| `project.id` | yes | Stable semantic project identity. |
| `project.name` | no | Human display name. |
| `defaultProfile` | no | Profile selected when `--profile` is omitted. Without it, a `profiles.default` entry is required. |
| `runtimeDir` | no | Repository-relative generated-state root; defaults to `.devfn`. |
| `ports` | no | Named `PortSpec` map. |
| `processes` | no | Named native process map. |
| `services` | no | Named Docker Compose service map. |
| `profiles` | yes | Named selections of processes/services plus non-secret environment and proxy choice. |
| `hostnames` | no | Explicit local hostname routes to named ports. |
| `resources` | no | Named backends and data stores with local or credential-free remote targets; see [resource targets and namespaces](#resource-targets-and-namespaces). |
| `prerequisites` | no | Required command/version diagnostics, optionally profile-scoped. |
| `environmentOutputs` | no | Repository-relative dotenv or JSON runtime files and owner-only permission modes. |
| `policy` | no | Repository-relative organization policy JSON path. |

Every repository-relative path rejects absolute paths, `..` escape, and runtime symlink escape. References to ports, processes, services, profiles, dependencies, and hostname targets must resolve during validation. An explicitly configured but missing policy is an error; only the conventional unconfigured policy path is optional.

## Ports

A port can specify `protocol` (`tcp` or `udp`), `preferred`, `range: [start, end]`, `exact`, `ephemeral`, `exposure` (`loopback` or `public`), conventional container `internal` port, contiguous `block` name, and exported `env` key.

- `exact: true` requires `preferred` and fails closed on collision.
- `ephemeral: true` cannot be combined with fixed preferences.
- Requirements sharing `block` receive a contiguous allocation.
- Public ports require `devfn up --allow-public`.

## Native processes

`adapter` is one of `command`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `turbo`, `wrangler`, `xcode`, or `extfn`. A process can specify `command`, package-manager `script`, repository-relative `cwd`, non-secret literal `env`, inherited `envAllowlist`, redacted `secretEnv`, named `ports`, `dependsOn`, `health`, `shutdownTimeoutMs`, and `exposure` (`local` or `public`).

Turbo, Wrangler, and ExtFn resolve project-local binaries with offline npm execution; pnpm runs through Corepack so the repository's `packageManager` pin is honored. Adapters never download a missing tool during startup. `doctor` reports the missing prerequisite instead. Discovery marks Yarn and Bun as proposed and emits no guessed npm process; add an explicit command adapter after review.

Local-process exposure verification requires `lsof` on macOS and Linux; Windows uses `netstat`. Run `devfn doctor` before startup to detect a missing listener-inspection tool.

Sensitive-looking keys cannot be literal manifest values. Numbered keys such as `API_TOKEN2` and compact names ending in an unambiguous credential word such as `MYPASSWORD`, `GITHUBTOKEN`, `MYAPIKEY`, or `MYACCESSKEY` follow the same rule. They must be inherited by name in `envAllowlist` and repeated in `secretEnv`, which activates streaming redaction before logs are persisted. PostgreSQL `PGPASSWORD` and qualified `pg_pass`/`pg_pwd` casing variants follow this rule. URL userinfo and credential-bearing headers such as `Authorization: Bearer` are rejected in resolved literals and argv, including when assembled from templates. Curl short-option clusters and cookie assignments receive the same validation; ordinary `--cookie theme=dark` and `--cookie=theme=dark` values are allowed. Public processes require `--allow-public`.

## Compose services

A service uses `adapter: "compose"`, Compose `service`, optional repository-relative `file`, project-name prefix, named host-port-to-container-port mappings, dependencies, health, `persistent`, non-secret `env`, `envAllowlist`, and `secretEnv`. DevFn adds a digest of the exact project prefix and opaque owner to the Compose project name, keeping separate accepted prefixes and owners isolated.

DevFn writes a generated override with loopback host mappings unless the named port explicitly selects public exposure. It starts only the requested service with `--no-deps`. Services declaring `secretEnv` use Docker's `none` logging driver and therefore cannot use log-pattern health checks. Ordinary cleanup stops/removes only invocation-owned containers and never passes a volume-deletion flag.

## Health checks

- HTTP: `{ type: "http", port: "app", path: "/health", expectedStatus: 200, timeoutMs: 120000 }`
- TCP: `{ type: "tcp", port: "postgres" }`
- Command: `{ type: "command", command: ["node", "scripts/ready.mjs"] }`
- Log: `{ type: "log", pattern: "ready on" }`

HTTP URLs are returned only for explicitly routed hostnames or ports named by HTTP health checks. Other services remain transport allocations visible through `devfn ports`; DevFn does not invent an HTTP URL for a database or arbitrary TCP listener.

## Startup endpoint and template resolution

`@devfn/core` exports `resolveEndpointTemplates({ config, plan, ownerId, ports, composeNetworks? })`. It is a pure resolver: `ownerId` is an opaque lifecycle owner supplied by the caller, and `ports` contains the selected profile's leased port numbers. `composeNetworks` maps selected service names to effective Docker network names. Supply it to publish Compose DNS URLs; absent network evidence omits those URLs and rejects references to them. The orchestrator reads the effective networks from `docker compose config` before creating state. It returns generated values, the profile environment, direct URLs, and resolved environment and command arguments for each selected node. The current CLI supplies its existing worktree instance ID as the owner. Callers of the resolver may use more than one owner per checkout. The resolver does not derive an owner from a path or start resources.

For each selected port, DevFn generates `DEVFN_PORT_<NAME>` (uppercase, punctuation replaced by `_`) and its configured `ports.<name>.env` alias. An HTTP health port, or a selected proxy hostname target, also gets `DEVFN_URL_<NAME>` as a direct loopback endpoint for host processes and owner-only output files. For Compose services on the same Compose project network, that key instead names the sibling service and its internal port, such as `http://web:8080`; `composeUrls` exposes these container-context values separately from `directUrls`. The leased host port remains in `DEVFN_PORT_<NAME>`. A route's HTTPS setting does not change its direct HTTP upstream; an explicitly direct HTTPS health endpoint retains HTTPS. Once all nodes are ready, the receipt's public `urls` may prefer installed proxy routes. A TCP or UDP allocation without an HTTP declaration has no invented URL.

Generated reserved values cannot be overridden. Profile literals establish defaults; a process or service literal with the same exact key wins for that node. Differently cased keys that collide after case folding are rejected. Selected inherited keys and platform base keys follow the same case-folded collision rule before startup, so macOS, Linux and Windows resolve the same map. Profile references resolve against generated and profile values before node overrides, so a node override does not retroactively change another profile value. The generated `DEVFN_*` namespace is reserved. `HOST` is reserved in profiles and local native processes: a local native process always receives `HOST=DEVFN_HOST=127.0.0.1`. An explicitly public native process may set or inherit `HOST` after public exposure is authorized. A Compose service may set `HOST` to its container bind address, including `0.0.0.0`. Local native node values, command argv and command-health argv may reference either generated bind key. These local process bind keys are not profile or Compose template inputs. Port environment aliases cannot use reserved keys. Colliding normalized port keys are rejected. The owner-only environment output file contains the resolved profile and generated non-secret values; node-specific values go only to that node.

Use `{{env.NAME}}` to refer explicitly to a generated or previously declared environment key in a profile value, node value, process `command` argument, package-manager `script`, or command-health argument. References inside each environment map may be forward references; cycles and missing references fail before any lease, file, process, or service mutation, while a self-reference to a generated port alias resolves to its generated value. Profile values can refer to generated values; node values and argv can also refer to resolved profile and node values. Compose service environment references use the container-context URL for sibling services; Compose command-health argv runs on the host and uses host-side direct URLs. Inherited `envAllowlist` values are delivered only through the existing process or Compose secret channel and cannot be template sources. Sensitive keys must be declared in `secretEnv`; credential values must not be placed in literals or argv. Empty or NUL argv values and malformed `{{...}}` references are rejected for all selected command sources. All other characters, including `$`, backticks, semicolons, pipes and ampersands, stay literal argv data; DevFn does not invoke a shell.

HTTP readiness that names a leased `port` probes its direct loopback URL at startup, status and retry, even when a `url` is also configured. The configured URL's path and query are retained; an HTTPS proxy route uses its direct HTTP upstream, while a genuinely direct HTTPS endpoint keeps HTTPS. A separate `path` is checked for credentials and validated against the configured URL origin before a leased origin is substituted, then appended by the existing URL path rule. URL-only readiness remains an explicit URL check, except that a URL aimed at a selected proxy route is rejected before startup: that route is installed only after nodes are ready. Compose interpolation receives the same resolved generated, profile and service values before `docker compose up`; Compose files must explicitly map those values into container `environment` entries when the container needs them. Each Compose service receives container-context sibling URLs only for services in the same owner-specific project with a shared effective Compose network. The default network counts when Compose assigns it; disjoint explicit networks and network namespace modes do not provide sibling DNS. Independent projects are allowed; an unreachable reference is rejected before mutation. An unmanaged pre-existing container is reused only when its effective environment matches the current Compose configuration, allowing only unchanged image defaults beyond the current keys; removed generated, profile, and service literals are rejected before startup. A native dependent can use a Compose service's leased host URL after that service becomes ready. URL userinfo and sensitive query, fragment or path assignment keys in manifest environment, argv, or effective health URLs are rejected without printing credentials, including URL forms normalized by Node's URL parser and percent-encoded values; credential argv flags such as `--token` are also rejected. Aliases `key`, `pass`, `pwd`, `auth`, `sig`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, and `credential` are sensitive at separator or camel/acronym boundaries, including qualified forms such as `db_password`, `DB_PASS`, and `DBSig`. Compact forms use the documented qualifiers in the core package README; ordinary words such as `monkey` and `compass` remain data. Pass credentials through `envAllowlist` and `secretEnv`. A ready receipt fingerprints declared startup inputs, selected port declarations, and the effective Compose service and referenced volume, network and config definitions. Compose resolves default and include-scoped interpolation and env files before fingerprinting; inherited host variables in selected Compose source require an explicit envAllowlist entry, and credential-named and secretEnv values are redacted before hashing. An effective source or env-file change degrades status and causes a safe owned restart on retry; changes discarded by Compose merge rules and byte-equivalent restoration retain the same fingerprint. Missing optional Compose env files are allowed; required files must exist. Existing v0.1 receipts without startup or port-spec fingerprints keep their prior readiness path.

For native commands, package scripts and command-health argv, a colon-delimited credential pair following `--user`, `--username`, `--proxy-user`, `-u` or `-U` is rejected in split, equals and attached forms. Plain user names remain valid. Percent-encoded credential URLs and headers are also rejected; encoding does not turn them into safe non-secret literals. This inspection does not invoke a shell or alter argument bytes.

Form arguments with credential-named fields and JSON bodies with credential-named keys are rejected in those same three argv sources, including nested objects, JSON-escaped keys, percent-encoded bodies, incomplete JSON bodies and shell-quoted JSON in package scripts. Ordinary non-secret JSON remains argv data. Deliver credentials through `envAllowlist` and `secretEnv` instead of embedding them in a command or readiness check.

Before reusing an unmanaged Compose container with `--no-recreate`, DevFn also compares Compose's effective service config hash with the hash persisted on that container. A changed command, published port, image, or other startup setting is rejected even when the environment is unchanged. Missing or malformed hash evidence fails closed before `up`.

## Profiles and hostnames

Profiles select named processes/services, add non-secret environment, and opt into the shared proxy with `proxy: true`. Dependencies are included transitively and started topologically. Cycles fail before mutation.

A hostname maps a route name to `target`, optional `hostname` template, `tls` (`off` or `internal`), and optional `profiles` filter. Templates accept `{project}` and `{instance}`. The route uses a stable DNS-safe component derived from an opaque owner; owners differing only by case receive distinct route names; the original owner value remains in ownership records and `DEVFN_INSTANCE_ID`. A configured static hostname receives an owner-derived label before `.localhost`, so two owners cannot publish the same route. Every resolved name must end in `.localhost` unless the route explicitly refers to a machine-registered domain.

`devfn domains register dev.example.test --tls internal` records a user-owned development domain in the machine state directory, bound to the current repository identity and project. Registration requires every current name-resolution answer for the domain to be loopback, so a reserved name such as `dev.example.test` must already resolve to loopback through local DNS or a hosts-file entry; a new or changed selected route must also resolve exclusively to loopback before startup and Caddy reload. Existing routes stay installed when another instance stops, even if their DNS later becomes unavailable. DNS with no answers, mixed local/public answers, or a nonloopback answer fails closed for route activation. The command does not edit DNS, `/etc/hosts`, the OS resolver, or a trust store. `devfn domains list` and `devfn domains unregister <domain>` inspect or remove registrations; removal refuses domains with active or pending routes. A registration cannot contain or be contained by any other registration, including one owned by the same repository. Public routing and remote targets have separate contracts.

A manifest can select `domain: "dev.example.test"` only after explicit machine registration. `host` optionally chooses a single DNS label shared by several path routes; otherwise the route key is used. Registered host labels can contain at most 40 characters. The worktree hostname is `<host>-<readable-worktree-name>-<stable-suffix>.<domain>`, with a 20-hex-character digest of the canonical worktree path as the suffix. The readable worktree name is shortened as needed so the whole first label fits DNS's 63-character limit; the suffix is always kept intact, so a long worktree directory name appears truncated in its hostname. The primary Git worktree also gets `<host>.<domain>` as its canonical alias. Both forms use one label under the domain, so one wildcard certificate can cover them. The suffix makes collisions between same-named worktrees extremely unlikely without depending on activation order. A registered route inherits its TLS mode from the machine registration; the manifest cannot override it. Default `.localhost` routes and their v0.1 owner-derived names remain unchanged.

`path` defaults to `/`, with `match: "prefix"`; `match: "exact"` selects only that path. A prefix matches its segment boundary (`/api` and `/api/...`, not `/apix`). `stripPrefix: true` strips a non-root prefix before proxying. Exact routes precede prefixes; longer prefixes precede shorter ones. Duplicate host/path/match routes fail before Caddy reload, and a host with only selected paths returns 404 elsewhere. All upstreams remain loopback.

Internal TLS uses the existing Caddy internal CA. Clients must explicitly trust that CA if they need verified HTTPS; DevFn never installs it. Selected TLS hosts redirect HTTP to HTTPS, while unknown HTTP hosts return 404. `--tls certificate --cert /absolute/cert.pem --key /absolute/key.pem` uses explicit PEM files. DevFn validates the key pair, validity dates, and DNS subject alternative name coverage of every generated hostname before publishing a route; a legacy common name alone does not count. A wildcard certificate may be needed for worktree names; a certificate for the registered base alone is insufficient. DNS-01 is rejected until a validated provider adapter is available. There is no implicit ACME, public certificate issuance, or CA installation.

## Resource targets and namespaces

`resources` declares the backends and data stores a profile can select, independently of which code runs locally. Each resource has a `kind` (`service`, `database`, `broker`, `cache`, `object-store` or `browser`) and named `targets`. A local target names the lifecycle node and one of its declared ports (`{ node, port, scheme?, path? }`). A remote target is a credential-free URL (`{ url }`). Remote URLs reject userinfo, queries, fragments, path assignments and percent-encoded data, which clients would decode into those forms. Non-HTTP schemes need an explicit port. Credentials are never manifest values. `secrets: { password: "DB_PASSWORD" }` names a host environment variable, and every consumer must already receive it through `envAllowlist` and `secretEnv`. DevFn records only the variable name and whether it is present.

A process or Compose service lists the resources it consumes in `resources`. Native processes, readiness commands and environment outputs use the host-side values. Every selected Compose service receives a resource's namespace values, which name state rather than a listener. Endpoint values depend on what a container reaches on its networks, and DevFn plans and checks only consumers' views, so only a consumer receives `_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_ENDPOINT` and `_URL`. The Compose provider of a selected local target receives the addresses it advertises, `_HOST_ENDPOINT` and `_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT`, without consuming itself. A template, a profile environment value resolved for a Compose service or a Compose interpolation of a value that service does not receive fails with `DEVFN_RUNTIME_INVALID`, naming the service, the resource and the reason. Profile environment values are resolved for every selected service, so a profile environment that references an endpoint value fails while a Compose service that does not consume it, such as its provider, is selected. Reference endpoint values from consumers' `env` instead. A profile selects a target with `profiles.<name>.resources: { <resource>: <target> }`; otherwise the resource's `defaultTarget` applies. A `defaultTarget` is the manifest author's explicit selection, including a remote one; the plan records it as `selectedBy: "defaultTarget"` with its manifest field, and any profile can select another target. A selected local target adds its provider node to the profile and starts it before its consumers. A remote selection starts nothing. Two clients can therefore share one backend, use different backends, or use a remote backend, and a local backend can use an explicitly selected remote database, without editing the processes. Target selection does not depend on whether the consumer runs natively or in Compose, and it never implies public exposure. `--allow-public` remains a separate confirmation, and remote access is a separate selection.

Validation happens before any lease, file, process or service changes. Unknown resources or targets, consumed resources without a selected target, names that normalize to the same key, generated-key collisions, consumption cycles (`DEVFN_DEPENDENCY_CYCLE`), local targets whose port the provider does not declare, and colliding namespaces on the same listener all fail. A collision that depends on a port number DevFn has not leased yet, such as a remote loopback URL naming the port a provider will lease, can only be detected under the lifecycle lock after reservation; that lease is then released and nothing starts. Ports with `exact: true` are known before reservation, so their collisions fail first. When a selected Compose service provides, consumes or references a resource, DevFn reads effective Compose networks before any state is created. Manifest errors use `DEVFN_CONFIG_INVALID`; selection and topology errors use `DEVFN_RESOURCE_INVALID`. Template references are still checked by the endpoint resolver, so a missing `{{env.DEVFN_RESOURCE_*}}` reference fails with its usual `DEVFN_RUNTIME_INVALID` missing-reference error.

Selected values join the generated values and use the existing template syntax and precedence. Every resource except a browser resource emits `DEVFN_RESOURCE_<NAME>_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_ENDPOINT` and, when a scheme is known, `_URL`. Native processes, readiness commands and environment outputs receive `127.0.0.1` with the leased port. A Compose consumer receives the provider's service name and internal port when both are in the same Compose project and share an effective network. Otherwise it receives the platform host gateway with the leased port: `host.docker.internal` on macOS and Windows (Docker Desktop). Linux has no implicit host gateway, so a Compose consumer of a host-loopback target fails instead of receiving `127.0.0.1`, which inside a container is the container itself. A remote target on any loopback spelling (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` including shorthand such as `127.1`, `0.0.0.0`, `[::1]`, `[::]` or an IPv4-mapped form, in any URL scheme and with or without a trailing dot) is treated the same way. A `*.localhost` remote target, such as the DevFn proxy, routes by its name, so DevFn never rewrites it to the gateway and a Compose consumer of one fails. For the same reason a Compose service that provides a selected resource cannot be named with a loopback spelling or a `*.localhost` name, which every container resolves to itself; manifests that select no resource from it keep any service name. Local targets also emit `_HOST_ENDPOINT` (`127.0.0.1:<leased>`), and Compose-provided targets also emit `_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT` (`<service>:<internal>`), so a broker can advertise both listeners. Native processes and the Compose provider receive them. Compose consumers do not, because host loopback inside a container is the container itself.

Namespaces are isolated by default. An isolated namespace appends an opaque token derived from the lifecycle owner and the runtime identity, so concurrent runtimes never share data by accident. The runtime identity is a random value that DevFn records as `runtime-id` in its state directory. It is created when a manifest with resources first starts there, after preflight validation, by linking a complete, flushed file into place, so a reader never sees a partial identity. Like DevFn's lock and registry files, this requires a state directory with hard links; elsewhere `up` fails before recording anything and asks for a local `--state-dir`. Checkouts at the same path on different machines, devcontainers or CI runners therefore get distinct namespaces. One runtime keeps its namespaces across restarts while its state directory remains. Removing `runtime-id` renames every isolated namespace. `namespace: { base?, sharing: "shared" }` uses `base` unchanged and is the only way to share. Database resources emit `_DATABASE` (`<base>_<token>`). With `level: "schema"` and a fixed `database`, they also emit `_SCHEMA`. Caches emit `_PREFIX` (`<base>:<token>:`), and object stores emit `_PREFIX` (`<base>/<token>/`). Brokers emit `_TOPIC_<TOPIC>` (`<base>.<token>.<topic>`) and `_CONSUMER_GROUP`. Topics and the consumer group always share one namespace, so an isolated runtime cannot join another runtime's group or read its topics. Browser resources declare `cookies` and `storageKeys` and emit `_COOKIE_<NAME>` and `_STORAGE_<NAME>`. Two selected resources of the same kind cannot overlap namespaces on the same listener. Object-store namespaces are the target URL path followed by the prefix, compared by path segment: `/bucket` with base `a` and `/bucket/a` with base `b` overlap (`/bucket/a/` holds `/bucket/a/b/`), while `/bucket` and `/bucket2` do not. Listeners are compared by the endpoints each receiving context resolves, not by port name, URL scheme or how a target is written. The host side always counts, and so does each Compose service that consumes the resource. A local provider is its port, its leased loopback port and, for a Compose provider, its container port. A remote target is what the host resolves (any loopback spelling is the loopback port; another host is its canonical name). Every target, local or remote, is also what each Compose consumer resolves for it. Inside a consumer, the host gateway is the loopback port, and a Docker DNS name is the container port of every selected service that answers it on a network the consumer joins, in any project: its service name or `container_name` on any network it joins, or an alias it declares on that network, because Docker DNS resolves these names across projects on a shared network. So `postgres://` and `postgresql://` to one host are one listener. So are a URL `redis://redis:6379` and a Compose `redis` provider on a network the consumer joins, even from another project, and `host.docker.internal:<leased>` and the provider that leases that port. The same service name or alias only on networks the consumer does not join is another listener. A name no selected service answers, such as an external host, is compared by its canonical name. A name the consumer maps itself through a `links` alias, `external_links` or `extra_hosts` bypasses Docker DNS, so a resource endpoint using it fails with `DEVFN_RESOURCE_INVALID`; only the container host gateway may be mapped that way. Which services a name reaches is decided with the effective networks and names that `docker compose config` reports before any state is created, never the provisional default networks. A Compose consumer's endpoint must also name exactly one listener, whatever the resource kind and namespaces: when a provider's service name also reaches another selected Compose service that answers it on a network the consumer joins, or a remote host names two such services, Docker DNS may answer with either, so planning fails with `DEVFN_RESOURCE_INVALID` naming the resource, the consumer and the competing services. A provider's own container port is known in every pass, so two port names on one container port collide before any state.

`planResources({ config, plan, ownerId, runtimeId?, ports, provisionalPorts?, composeNetworks?, provisionalNetworks?, platform?, containerHostGateway? })` returns the redacted plan. `containerHostGateway` replaces the platform host gateway (`null` disables it) and must be a bare hostname, IPv4 address or bracketed IPv6 address that is not a loopback spelling; userinfo, a scheme, a port, a path or whitespace fail with `DEVFN_RESOURCE_INVALID`, and the rejected value is not echoed. `provisionalPorts` marks `ports` as preflight placeholders, and `provisionalNetworks` marks `composeNetworks` as placeholders, so which services a consumer reaches by name waits for effective networks. It contains each selected target, how it was selected, its provider or credential-free remote URL, its consumers, its namespace, its secret references, and every emitted value with its source (`manifest`, `lease`, `compose`, `host-gateway` or `namespace`) and the manifest field or platform that produced it. The orchestrator passes the plan to `resolveEndpointTemplates` as `resources` and records it in the receipt. `devfn up --json` and `devfn restart --json` print the plan as recorded: it holds no credential, so the CLI's key-based redaction, which still applies to the rest of the output, does not mask resource, secret-reference or cookie names. The resolver applies its decoded URL credential checks to every resource value, whether or not a template references it. A running lifecycle is reused only while its selected targets, namespaces and values are unchanged, including from a receipt written without startup fingerprints, such as a DevFn v0.1 receipt. A `${DEVFN_RESOURCE_*}` reference that appears only in a Compose file must name a value that service receives: a typo, an unselected resource or the `_URL` of a target without a scheme fails with the usual `DEVFN_RUNTIME_INVALID` missing-reference error, and an unreachable value with its reason, before any state is created. A fallback form such as `${DEVFN_RESOURCE_<NAME>_URL:-<default>}` is not a reference while the value is unset. Manifests without `resources` resolve exactly as before. This release plans topology only. Resource ownership, consumer leases, teardown, persistence and data reset are not part of it.

## Organization policy

`devfn.policy.json` supports `fallbackRange`, `hostnameSuffix`, and entries with `name`, exactly one of `port`/`range`, `kind` (`protected`, `preferred`, or `excluded`), optional `project`, and `description`. `devfn ports report` combines the policy with the entire machine registry into Markdown; it is not limited to the current project or profile. `--output` must remain inside the repository.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/core.md path:/docs/reference/core -->
# @devfn/core

> Source package guide for @devfn/core.


Builds dependency-ordered lifecycle plans, reserves ports before mutation, starts Compose and native resources, verifies readiness, registers shared proxy routes, emits machine-readable receipts, and rolls back only resources created by the failing invocation. The public `resolveEndpointTemplates({ config, plan, ownerId, ports, composeNetworks?, composeReferences? })` API accepts an opaque owner chosen by its caller; see the [startup endpoint contract](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/configuration.md#startup-endpoint-and-template-resolution).

**Replacement and rollback.** Ready-instance replacement checks sibling leases and route ownership, resolves the selected configuration, reserves its ports and activates its Caddy routes while the old service is still available. A failure at any of those steps leaves the old lifecycle, receipt, leases and routes unchanged. Replacement then stops the old lifecycle before it starts the new one, because both normally use the same ports and Compose project. If a later step fails, such as edited source exiting or readiness timing out, DevFn does not relaunch the old processes from the working tree, which may no longer contain the old source. Their leases and routes are released, the failed receipt and the error record that the prior invocation was stopped, and status reports `failed`. If the old lifecycle cannot be stopped, nothing new starts; its receipt becomes `degraded` and keeps its leases until `devfn down`.

**Teardown and reconciliation.** Teardown (`down`, restart, replacement and failed-start cleanup) stops a recorded process and its process group only by its verified start identity, and waits until the whole group is gone (an exited member a container PID 1 never reaps counts as gone, but only when every member can be listed: an unreadable `/proc` entry or a `/proc` mounted with `hidepid` leaves the group possibly running); an exited wrapper whose group is empty, or a readable different start identity, proves it gone, while a wrapper that exited while its application still runs in its group, a live PID whose identity cannot be read, including one still running after a stop was refused because its identity could not be read at that moment, is a cleanup error that leaves the lifecycle `degraded` with its leases, routes and owner journal, and `up` then refuses to start a duplicate. Teardown also reconciles the receipt with the registry owner journal: journaled processes the receipt does not list are stopped by verified identity, journaled containers it does not list must be verified gone, and an interrupted Compose launch is stopped through its Compose project and service labels, leaving containers that ran before it. `docker compose up` runs through a gated launcher whose PID and start identity are journaled before it may run, so an unrecorded launcher never ran Compose. An interrupted launch resolves only after its launcher is stopped by verified identity and no process in its process group remains, and then only after a label scan, repeated after a settle period and re-reading the state of containers already stopped, finds nothing the launch created and nothing it started running, because the Docker daemon may still finish a request the killed launcher sent (a request delayed beyond the final scan is not observable, and a container it creates after `down` reports stopped is not tracked by DevFn); a launcher whose identity cannot be read, or whose group outlived it, keeps the launch unresolved even when Docker lists no container yet. On Windows, which has no process groups, only the launcher itself is checked. No startup environment values or `secretEnv` values are persisted for replacement.

**Routing and recovery.** The machine routing lock covers ownership changes; health probes, process/Compose stops and readiness waits run under the instance lock. A down refreshes its `stopping` claim while it runs. After an interrupted down, sibling worktrees reconcile verified-dead owners once the claim expires, and the next `up` or `restart` in that worktree finishes the stop first. Legacy v0.1 ready receipts are replaced the same way. Replacement reconciles this worktree's committed and pending Caddy routes with the final selection even when the prior receipt recorded none, so routes left by an interrupted replacement are removed when the profile no longer selects a proxy; until then their target ports and listener claims stay unavailable to sibling worktrees. If route activation or a later pre-teardown step fails, DevFn restores this worktree's routes as they were before activation only when its committed or pending route state changed; a candidate Caddy rejected before any change reports its own error. Certificate routes are restored with the private certificate snapshots they were served with, captured before activation, never from their source PEM files, which may since have been removed or rotated; a replacement whose served snapshot is missing or modified is refused before anything changes. If that rollback itself fails, the error says so (`routesRestored: false`); it is never reported as routes kept. When the prior teardown was refused, the prior receipt is `degraded` and lists the failed restore among its cleanup errors. When the replacement's own registry record could not be written, the prior receipt file is left unchanged, and `status` reports the lifecycle `degraded` because its routes are no longer the ones served. The captured snapshots live only in the replacing command, and activation prunes snapshots no committed route uses, so a replacement killed between route activation and the prior teardown cannot restore them. The prior lifecycle keeps running but its routes are no longer served, and `status` reports it `degraded`; `devfn down` stops it, removes every route of this worktree, including the replacement's, and ends the interrupted invocation. A later `up` validates the certificate source files again: a removed or invalid one fails with `DEVFN_DOMAIN_CERT_INVALID` until it is fixed. Readiness, and therefore whether `up` reports `DEVFN_ALREADY_RUNNING` or replaces a lifecycle, is judged under the proxy lock so a sibling's in-flight Caddy reload is not mistaken for a dead proxy. `recoverOrphanedProxyRoutes`, used by `devfn ports gc`, removes routes left by worktrees whose recorded process and container owners are all verified dead; an interrupted start whose detached services still run keeps its routes, even after the next lifecycle marked it failed without its receipt listing them, a live owner whose start identity cannot be read keeps them too, and a ready lifecycle that died stays recoverable after earlier reconciles collected its leases. A Caddy that DevFn started but that failed to confirm its listeners is stopped, and its exit observed, before the failure returns; if its exit cannot be confirmed, the failed lifecycle keeps its listener claim. Replacement preflight renders activated sibling routes with their private certificate snapshots, as activation does.

`resolveEndpointTemplates` runs before startup. Generated `DEVFN_*` keys are reserved, generated port aliases take precedence over same-key literals, and native loopback bind values are fixed; profile references resolve before node overrides, and explicit `{{env.NAME}}` references resolve in their selected consumer context. Native processes receive host-loopback `DEVFN_URL_*` values. Compose services receive sibling DNS URLs only when the caller supplies effective Compose network names for both services and they share a network in the same owner-specific project. The orchestrator obtains those names and selected raw Compose interpolation references before creating state. A reference in either a manifest template or selected Compose source to an unreachable sibling URL or native loopback URL fails before state mutation. A service without such a reference omits unreachable sibling URLs.

Compose command readiness executes on the host. Its argv and `readinessEnvironment` therefore use host-loopback URLs, while `environment` retains the container URLs used for Compose interpolation. Startup, status, and retry use the same host-side values. HTTP readiness checks the configured URL and path for credentials before replacing a selected proxy origin with the directly reachable leased endpoint. It preserves the exact leased port even when an HTTPS route is probed over direct HTTP. Credential-bearing manifest values must use `envAllowlist` and `secretEnv`; they are excluded from endpoint resolutions and receipts.

The host command-readiness process inherits explicitly allowlisted values, including `secretEnv` credentials, at probe time. Other readiness types do not receive those credentials. The values stay out of resolved endpoint plans and receipt fields. A changed or missing inherited credential can make command readiness fail until the host environment is restored. Inherited host values do not enter startup fingerprints; declared key names do.

Template syntax and credential-bearing source values are checked before substitution. Credential names include `key`, `pass`, `pwd`, `auth`, `sig`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, and `credential` aliases, with separator or camel/acronym boundaries; compact names use documented qualifiers `api`, `app`, `auth`, `aws`, `client`, `db`, `database`, `google`, `oauth`, `pg`, `server`, `service`, `session`, `user`, `xamz`, and `xgoog`. This includes `PGPASSWORD` and qualified PostgreSQL password names. Credential-bearing headers are rejected after template expansion. Other ordinary compact words remain data. A referenced opaque owner remains literal data even when its bytes resemble template or credential syntax. Generated route hostnames and Compose project names include a digest of the exact owner bytes, so case-distinct owners have separate namespaces while receipts retain the original owner. Compose project comparison uses the same canonical name as Compose startup: its readable prefix is normalized, and a digest of the exact prefix distinguishes case and punctuation. Ready receipts fingerprint declared environment and command inputs, selected port declarations, and secret key names without hashing inherited host values. Status reports a changed startup snapshot as degraded, and `up` safely cleans up the owned lifecycle before restarting it with the selected configuration. Older receipts without a startup digest retain v0.1 readiness behavior.

Native command, package script and command-health argv are also checked as vectors. `--user`, `--username`, `--proxy-user`, `-u` and `-U` accept ordinary names, but a colon-delimited credential pair is rejected in split, equals or attached forms. Percent-encoded URL and header credentials are checked before any startup mutation. The resolver inspects these forms without splitting or interpreting the argv used for execution.

HTTP readiness runs against the leased upstream port before a selected Caddy route is installed. For a route that strips a path prefix, configure health with the upstream path (for example `/ready` for a published `/api/ready`); a health URL through the stripped published path fails preflight. Status treats an older receipt with stale Caddy listener ports as degraded, and the next `up` refreshes that instance's published URLs. Status is also degraded when the recorded Caddy owner has exited, a listener port stops accepting, or the committed routes differ from the receipt, for example after a replacement was interrupted between route activation and its receipt write; the next `up` replaces the lifecycle and restores matching routes.

Form and query options (`--data*`, `--form*`, `--url-query`, `-d`, `-F`) also reject credential-named `name=value` and `name@file` inputs in split, equals, attached and percent-encoded forms. Ordinary field names and literal shell metacharacters remain data.
Credential-named assignments inside attached long-option values, such as `--env=DB_PASSWORD=value` or `--build-arg=PGPASSWORD=value`, follow the same secret-channel rule. This includes encoded delimiters and name-only forwarding values; ordinary assignments such as `--env=NODE_ENV=development` remain argv data.
Structured argv checks inspect XML element and attribute names outside quoted attribute values. A `>` inside a quoted value does not end the tag, and credential-named attributes after it are rejected before startup; ordinary quoted text remains argv data.
