# Migration guide

> Adopt DevFn without losing existing scripts, outputs, or Compose data.


1. Preserve all existing scripts and Compose data.
2. Run `devfn init`, inspect confirmed versus proposed detections, then rerun with `--yes` only when the preview is truthful.
3. Edit the manifest so every command, dependency, port, profile, and health check is explicit.
4. Run `devfn doctor --trust`; address missing runtimes and exact-port conflicts.
5. Before the first start, back up every pre-existing file targeted by `environmentOutputs[].path`; DevFn overwrites configured outputs and cannot restore prior contents.
6. Start with a minimal profile and compare it with the existing manual startup flow.
7. Add full, OAuth, test, or docs profiles incrementally. Public tunnels must remain explicit.
8. Verify `devfn down` preserves databases and volumes before adopting it as the daily command.

Rollback by running `devfn down`, then inspect `runtimeDir` and every `environmentOutputs[].path` in the manifest before removing generated files. The default generated location is `.devfn/`, but custom paths may live elsewhere. Preserve any target that existed before DevFn adoption; cleanup does not know whether a configured output replaced user-owned content. Finally remove the DevFn manifest and continue using the preserved original scripts. Docker volumes and source configuration are not deleted.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/ports.md path:/docs/reference/ports -->
# @devfn/ports

> Source package guide for @devfn/ports.


Machine-local, lock-protected port leases with worktree instance identity, exact/preferred/range/ephemeral allocation, stale reconciliation, listener discovery, Docker mapping discovery, and generated inventory reports. Reports enumerate the complete machine registry, including other projects and profiles, and are not a current-selection view.

Selected proxy routes claim Caddy's listener ports across TCP and UDP. One rule retires a claim, whether it was abandoned by an expired command, left by an interrupted lifecycle, or kept by a failed one: neither committed nor pending proxy state contains the instance's routes, and direct evidence proves that no listener remains. Successful socket inspection is not enough because a non-dumpable owner (a setcap Caddy on Linux) hides its sockets: every claimed port must refuse TCP connections on 127.0.0.1 and, when available, ::1, and must bind for both TCP and UDP (Caddy's HTTP/3) on each of those addresses. A refused connection alone is never proof, because a firewall rule can refuse connections to a listening port. A bind that is denied, as for an unprivileged Linux user on 80 or 443, proves nothing, so that claim stays until a verified live Caddy owner's admin configuration excludes the port; a bind that fails for any other reason than an occupied address or a denial keeps the claim. A verified live owner may keep its admin listener after its last site is removed, but its live admin configuration must be readable and name no HTTP server listener on a claimed port; an absent, dead, or reused owner requires a free admin listener. Malformed route or owner state and unverified owner identity retain the claim for inspection. A healthy route or bound proxy listener keeps the ports protected while sibling worktrees start and stop.
Recovering an interrupted `planning` or `starting` invocation fails it but keeps its listener claim (`proxyClaimRetained`) unless that rule already holds. Releasing the last claim on a listener uses the same rule, so an invocation that ends with routes still in proxy state (for example after a failed replacement rollback) or while a Caddy it started may still listen (a failed start whose Caddy exit was not confirmed) keeps its claim the same way. Another running lifecycle of that instance claiming the same ports covers the claim; another instance's claim covers it only once this instance has no routes left. Garbage collection keeps such invocations until reconciliation retires their claims.
A TCP port targeted by another instance's committed or pending proxy route stays unavailable for TCP leases by every other instance, even after its lease ended and even when that instance already leases it, until a route transition replaces or removes that route; the routed instance itself may lease it again to repair the route. Routes carry HTTP over TCP only, so a UDP lease of the same number is not blocked by them. Each invocation journals its owners in the registry, which outlives a deleted worktree: a Compose launch is recorded with its project, service and pre-existing containers before Compose runs, then with its `docker compose up` launcher's PID and start identity before that launcher may run, and the process (PID and start identity) or container IDs right after the receipt lists them; a process command runs only after its identity is recorded, so an interrupted process launch never starts it. Ready lease owners are copied there too, so reconcile and gc of leases never erase them. `devfn ports gc` removes the routes of an instance only when it can take that instance's lifecycle lock (no command of it runs) and every recorded owner of its invocations, including failed and interrupted ones, is verified dead: a process whose PID and process group are both gone or whose readable start identity differs (a reused PID), or a container Docker reports missing; a recorded wrapper that exited while processes remain in its group may still run. A stopped invocation ended only after teardown verified every receipt and journal owner dead or stopped it by verified identity and resolved every launch; otherwise it stays `stopping` or `failed` and keeps its leases, routes and journal. A recently refreshed command, a launch with no recorded identity, a live owner, a live PID whose start identity cannot be read, an unreachable Docker endpoint, and a legacy running invocation with neither an owner journal nor a recorded owner all keep the routes; gc keeps a failed invocation while any of its recorded owners may run. Lease age and occupied target ports are never death evidence; an expired planned lease whose port is occupied becomes `externally-occupied`, not `stale`, and an active lease whose process identity cannot be read stays active. An `externally-occupied` lease keeps its invocation's listener claim only while one of that invocation's recorded owners may still run; once all are verified dead the occupant is foreign and the claim retires through the shared rule. Unreadable proxy route state fails reservation closed. Replacement preflight applies the same abandoned-claim recovery and routed-port rule before checking exact ports.
A stopping invocation, and a replacement holding its predecessor's leases, are protected only while their command refreshes them. Five minutes after the last refresh, reconciliation and claim recovery treat them like any other lease: a lease whose owner is verified dead becomes `stale` when its port is free and `externally-occupied` when the port is occupied, and a lease whose owner is live or ambiguous stays active.

**Locks.** Registry, domain and proxy mutations share a routing lock, so sibling claims cannot appear between replacement validation and route publication. Its holder is recognized under any spelling of the state directory. Every lock is taken by creating its directory, which never replaces a lock, including one an earlier release is still creating. The holder then publishes its owner record without replacing another holder's, and releases only a lock that records itself.

A routing lock whose holder is verified dead is recovered once its owner record is a minute old, within a waiter's three-minute budget; other locks wait five minutes. Recovery takes the lock over in place and never removes it, so no command can create the lock meanwhile. Once a holder is recorded, its owner record is never missing, so a creator that has not yet recorded itself cannot take the lock either. Only one command at a time may take over a given dead holder's record, and it replaces that record only while it is still the one judged dead. A command killed mid-takeover is superseded once it is verified dead, however many were killed before it, within the waiting command's budget. An owner record or takeover marker (`owner.takeover.*`) that cannot be read, or is not a well-formed DevFn owner record (a non-empty token, a positive integer PID and a parseable creation time), counts as a live command's and blocks recovery of that lock; remove it by hand once no DevFn command runs.

A lock without an owner record is taken only after five minutes, which is how long earlier releases also wait, and only if its creator has not recorded itself first. Such a lock is left by a creator killed before recording itself. Earlier releases still recover a stale lock by moving it aside, so one acting on an outdated judgment can hold the lock alongside a command of this release, as two earlier releases already can; stop older DevFn commands before relying on stale-lock recovery.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/processes.md path:/docs/reference/processes -->
# @devfn/processes

> Source package guide for @devfn/processes.


Native process groups, durable logs, HTTP/TCP/command/log readiness, PID-birth ownership checks, and graceful termination. It is deliberately browser- and artifact-model-neutral so ProbeFn can adopt it later without depending on DevFn orchestration.

## Gated launches

- `runGatedCommand` runs a command that creates outside resources only after its launcher identity has been recorded. The process wrapper never runs its command without the launch gate channel.
- On POSIX, `gatedLauncherStatus`/`stopGatedLauncher` resolve such a launch only once the launcher and its process group are gone. On Windows they judge and stop only the launcher and its current process tree, so they cannot confirm that a descendant which left that tree is gone.
- `runGatedCommand` redacts the values of `redactKeys` from the command's output and keeps at most `maxBuffer` bytes of each output stream, stopping the launcher's group as soon as either passes it.
- Once the command exits, it waits at most a bounded drain for output that a process it left behind still holds open, then stops that process's group, waiting a bounded time for it to exit and forcing it if needed. A finished command therefore never waits indefinitely on a leftover process. A failed stop is reported together with the command's own outcome, never instead of it.

## Process groups

- Every recorded process and launcher leads its own process group (POSIX), and `processGroupStatus` judges the whole group: a leader that exited while processes remain in its group is `unverified`, not gone, and a reused leader PID (a readable different start identity) proves the group gone, because a PID is not reused while its group exists.
- `stop` signals only a verified leader, waits until its whole group is gone (forcing members that ignore termination), and never signals a live PID whose start identity cannot be read or a leaderless group (`DEVFN_PROCESS_IDENTITY_UNVERIFIED`).
- The group is judged again immediately before each signal. POSIX offers no way to signal a group atomically with that check, but a group ID is not reused while any member remains, so the only exposure is a group that empties and whose ID a new group leader takes in the instant between the check and the signal.
- On Windows, which has no process groups, only the leader is judged and stopped with its process tree.

## Start identities

- Start identities do not depend on the caller's environment: on macOS the `ps` start time is read with `TZ=UTC0` and `LC_ALL=C`.
- A signature recorded by an earlier release in the caller's time zone and locale is never compared as text. It is decided by the record's own UTC time (a receipt process's `startedAt`, a lock's or trust ticket's `createdAt`, a Caddy owner's `startedAt`, a port lease owner's `recordedAt`), which DevFn writes only after reading a live owner's identity:
  - a process whose pinned UTC start is later than that time by more than two seconds is another process reusing the PID;
  - one that started no later than that time is the recorded process;
  - a record without a time, or a start later than it by at most two seconds (the allowance for wall-clock adjustment), is `unverified`.
- An earlier release's active port lease has no `recordedAt`, but its `updatedAt` was written at activation, just after its owner's identity was read, and stays unchanged while the lease is active, so the registry copies it to the owner's `recordedAt` before any transition; a lease whose PID was reused is then `stale` or `externally-occupied` as in earlier releases. Only a lease that already left `active` under an earlier release has no record time, and its owner stays `unverified`.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/proxy.md path:/docs/reference/proxy -->
# @devfn/proxy

> Source package guide for @devfn/proxy.


Maintains one lock-protected, DevFn-owned Caddy route registry.

- **Routes.** Generated configurations contain concrete `.localhost` or explicitly registered local-domain routes and loopback targets only, are validated before reload, and deny unknown HTTP hosts. Selected TLS hosts redirect HTTP to HTTPS; unknown hosts receive 404. If another Caddy owns the admin endpoint, DevFn refuses to replace its configuration. DevFn runs the Caddy found in an absolute `PATH` directory, never one found through a relative entry, and uses that one binary to validate, reload and run a configuration.
- **Listeners and ports.** Caddy binds to 127.0.0.1 and adds ::1 when the host supports it; DNS answers for any other address, including another 127/8 address, are rejected because Caddy does not bind them. macOS uses unprivileged loopback ports 8080 and 8443, so its published URLs include those nonstandard ports; Linux uses 80 and 443, so its URLs omit the port. Existing v0.1 services on these ports must be stopped and assigned another exact or preferred port before activating a proxy route. A conflict identifies the owning instance and service; DevFn does not reassign or stop it.
- **Linux privileges.** Linux requires permission to bind the privileged ports: either `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` at or below 80, or `cap_net_bind_service` granted to the Caddy binary with `setcap`. DevFn changes neither. A capability-bearing Caddy is non-dumpable, so same-user socket inspection cannot attribute its sockets; DevFn then accepts its recorded owner only when the PID start identity matches and the live admin configuration equals DevFn's committed configuration.
- **Activation and readiness.** A started Caddy counts as activated only after it confirms through `--pingback` that its whole configuration, including every HTTP and HTTPS listener, started; an answering admin endpoint alone is not enough. A failed bind therefore fails activation before a ready replacement is stopped. Instance readiness also requires the committed routes to equal the receipt's routes and the recorded Caddy owner to be alive, to run the configuration rendered from the committed (or journaled pending) route state as shown by its live admin configuration, and to accept connections on its listener ports.
- **TLS and DNS.** It never installs its internal CA in a trust store. Registered domains are bound to a repository and project in machine state. New or changed registered routes must resolve exclusively to available Caddy loopback binds, and explicit certificates must cover every route hostname through a DNS SAN. DNS verification fails closed after five seconds, so a stalled lookup cannot indefinitely hold the shared proxy lock.
- **Snapshots and rollback.** Activated explicit certificates are kept as private immutable snapshots so sibling cleanup can reload after a source file disappears. Stopping one instance can retain another instance's established routes when its DNS is temporarily unavailable. A pending activation with invalid DNS or certificate is rolled back to the last committed routes. A failed or timed-out reload does not prove Caddy kept its previous routes: the activation's journal stays, marked uncertain (`proxy-routes.pending.uncertain`), and its routes count as possibly live until a reload of the committed routes succeeds. That reload is tried at once and by the next routing command or route preflight, which rolls the activation back rather than replaying it. The journal is marked before it is published and reloaded, so this holds even when nothing can be written after the failure, and an interrupted activation is rolled back too; only an unmarked journal, such as one an earlier release left, is replayed. Like every transition and preflight, it leaves out routes of services verified gone, whose IDs and hostnames another owner may then take, and only the routes Caddy confirmed are committed. Until it succeeds, commands that change routes fail rather than treat its routes as gone. Removing or emptying an owner that no route state names changes no routes, so it never touches Caddy or another owner's journal.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/security.md path:/docs/reference/security -->
# Security contract

> Manifest trust, secret handling, local exposure, and ownership.


- Every DevFn manifest can declare lifecycle commands, so the CLI refuses to load JSON, TypeScript, or JavaScript until the user records trust for its exact digest with `--trust`. JSON is parsed directly from the verified bytes; executable manifests run from a private copy of those same bytes and must be self-contained, with imports and `require()` rejected so dependency files cannot bypass the digest boundary.
- Runtime children inherit a small base environment plus explicit `envAllowlist` entries. Sensitive-looking keys must also be listed in `secretEnv`; a detached wrapper redacts those effective values before native-process logs are persisted. Literal values are rejected only when their key looks sensitive, so review every manifest literal. Compose logging is disabled for services with `secretEnv` because Docker otherwise retains historical unredacted logs. Secrets are not persisted in the registry or lifecycle receipt.
- Generated environment and state files use owner-only modes (default `0600`); their directories use `0700`. Existing files are explicitly re-permissioned after each write.
- Local ports and proxy targets bind to loopback unless a manifest explicitly selects public exposure. Profiles containing public processes or ports require the separate `--allow-public` confirmation on every start. A public Cloudflare tunnel must never be inferred.
- Repository-relative process, Compose, runtime, policy, and output paths are validated against lexical and symlink path escape.
- PID ownership uses a birth signature where the host exposes one, read the same way whatever time zone or locale DevFn runs in (macOS `ps` is pinned to `TZ=UTC0 LC_ALL=C`); a signature an earlier release recorded in the caller's time zone is never compared as text, but judged by the record's own UTC time: a process that started after the record was written is a reused PID, one that started no later is the recorded owner, and a record without a time stays unverified. A process that started within two seconds after the record time, the allowance for wall-clock adjustment, is also unverified rather than reused: DevFn neither signals it nor retires its leases, routes or claims, and teardown reports a cleanup error until the PID is free or a later run can decide. An earlier release's active port lease is judged by its activation time, written just after its owner's identity was read. A recorded process is judged with its whole process group: when the recorded wrapper or launcher exited but processes remain in its group, DevFn treats it as possibly running, keeps its leases, routes, listener claims and owner journal, does not signal the leaderless group, and reports a cleanup error until it is gone. Stopping a verified process waits until its whole group is gone and forces members that ignore termination. A member that has exited but was not reaped (a zombie, as every orphan stays under a container PID 1 that does not reap) counts as gone: it runs nothing, and its PID and group ID cannot be reused until it is reaped. A member DevFn cannot list or signal counts as possibly running, so on Linux a group is proven gone only when every `/proc` entry can be read and parsed and `/proc` is not mounted with `hidepid`; otherwise it stays possibly running. Processes that leave their group (for example by `setsid`) and Windows process trees after their leader exits are outside this check. DevFn refuses to stop a reused PID, and never signals a live PID whose start identity cannot be read: `down`, restart and replacement then report a cleanup error, leave the receipt `degraded` and keep its leases, routes and owner journal until a later `down` can verify or stop it. Teardown also stops owners the registry journal records that the receipt does not list, and finds the containers of an interrupted Compose launch by its Compose project and service labels; a container that ran before the launch is left running. A process still running after its stop was refused on identity grounds is a cleanup error, not a stopped owner.
- Compose launches: `docker compose up` runs only after its launcher's identity is journaled, and an interrupted launch is resolved only once that launcher and every process in its process group are gone, so a Compose run that outlived DevFn cannot send Docker a new request after `down` reports stopped. The Docker daemon may still finish a create or start request the killed launcher had already sent, so the label scan then repeats, re-reading the state of every container it already stopped, and resolves only after a one-second settle period in which nothing the launch created remains and nothing it started runs; after five passes it reports a cleanup error and keeps the launch journal, leases and routes. A daemon request delayed beyond that final scan is not observable to DevFn: a container it creates after `down` reports stopped is outside this guarantee and is not tracked by DevFn.
- `down` stops only the exact worktree instance. Ordinary shutdown removes no persistent Docker volumes.
- `.localhost` remains the default hostname suffix. Other development domains require explicit machine registration for the repository and project; a repository manifest cannot register one. Each selected alias must resolve only to loopback, and registration does not change DNS, a hosts file, or the OS resolver. Public routing needs separate validation.
- DevFn manages only a Caddy process it started itself and refuses to overwrite an unrelated Caddy admin endpoint. Internal TLS uses Caddy's local CA without installing its trust root; clients must trust that CA explicitly. Explicit certificate mode requires a valid matching key and a DNS subjectAltName covering every selected alias before proxy reload. DNS-01 is unavailable until a validated adapter exists and is rejected rather than configured implicitly.
- Caddy listeners and ports:
  - Listener binding: Caddy binds only to available 127.0.0.1 and ::1 loopback interfaces. Registered DNS answers for other loopback addresses are rejected because Caddy does not bind them. If an external process occupies a listener, proxy startup fails rather than binding a public interface. DevFn runs the Caddy found in an absolute `PATH` directory, never one in a relative entry such as `.`, and validates, reloads and runs a configuration with that same binary.
  - Platform ports: on macOS, an unprivileged process cannot bind loopback port 80 or 443, so DevFn uses HTTP 8080 and HTTPS 8443 and includes those ports in published URLs and redirects. Linux uses 80 and 443, so its URLs omit the port; binding them requires `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` at or below 80 or `cap_net_bind_service` on the Caddy binary. DevFn does not change system permissions.
  - Owner verification: a setcap Caddy hides its sockets from same-user inspection, so DevFn verifies it by PID start identity and by comparing its live admin configuration with the committed one.
  - Claim retirement: a listener claim left by an expired, interrupted, or failed lifecycle is retired only after the instance has no committed or pending routes, TCP connections are refused and both TCP and UDP binds succeed on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, and a live owner's configuration excludes the port. A refused connection alone proves nothing, because a firewall rule can refuse connections to a listening port. A denied privileged bind can be cleared only when a verified owner's configuration excludes the port; any other bind failure keeps the claim.
  - `devfn ports gc`: removes proxy routes only for instances with no running command whose recorded process and container owners, including those of failed or interrupted invocations, are all verified dead; a live PID whose start identity cannot be read, lease age and occupied ports are not evidence.
  - Failed start and activation: activation succeeds only after Caddy confirms that every listener started. A failed Caddy start returns only after the Caddy DevFn spawned has exited; if it cannot be stopped, its owner record, when one was written, is kept, the error names its PID, and the failed lifecycle keeps its listener claim until the listener is proven gone. A failed or timed-out reload, or a spawned Caddy that does not exit, is never taken as proof that Caddy kept its previous routes: Caddy may already serve the candidate. Its activation journal stays, marked uncertain, and every reader of pending route state counts its routes as possibly live until a reload of the committed routes succeeds. After a failed reload, that reload is tried at once and by the next routing command; a spawned Caddy that does not exit is rolled back by the next routing command. Neither replays the activation, and a route preflight first rolls a marked journal back the same way, so a rejected activation never blocks another owner's routes once Caddy reloads. The journal is marked before it is published and before Caddy reloads or starts, so this holds even when nothing can be written after the failure, and an interrupted activation is rolled back too; only an unmarked journal, such as one an earlier release left, is replayed. Like every transition, it leaves out routes of services verified gone, which own no route ID or hostname for a transition or its preflight, and only the routes Caddy confirmed are committed; a recovered journal is likewise never rewritten before Caddy confirms it. While it fails, commands that change routes fail rather than treat the routes as gone. A lifecycle that no route state names changes no routes: its teardown never touches Caddy or another owner's journal, so it is not held by that journal. A lock left by a routing operation whose holder is verified dead is recovered after one minute, within the three minutes a waiting command allows. Locks are taken by creating their directory, which never replaces an existing lock, including one an earlier release is creating; its owner record is then added without replacing another holder's, and a holder removes only a lock recording itself. A stale lock is taken over in place, never removed first, and once a holder is recorded its owner record is never missing, so neither a new command nor a creator that has not yet recorded itself can take the lock meanwhile. Only one command at a time takes over a given dead holder's record, and only while it is still the record judged dead; a command killed mid-takeover is superseded once it is verified dead, however many were killed before it, within the waiting command's budget. An owner record or takeover marker that cannot be read, or is not a well-formed DevFn owner record, counts as a live command's and needs manual removal once no DevFn command runs. Earlier releases do not follow this rule and still move a stale lock aside to recover it, so one acting on an outdated judgment can hold the lock alongside a command of this release, as two earlier releases already can; stop older DevFn commands before relying on stale-lock recovery. A lock without an owner record, left by a creator killed before recording itself, is taken only after five minutes, the time earlier releases also wait for its creator to record itself.
  - Claims and migration: a profile with selected proxy routes claims both listener ports before service startup; existing sibling TCP or UDP leases on either port block that activation. While a proxy claim is active, other DevFn profiles cannot lease those ports. A TCP port that another instance's committed or pending route targets cannot be leased for TCP by any other instance, including one that already holds it, until that route is replaced or removed. To migrate an existing v0.1 service on a listener port, stop its profile, change its exact or preferred service port in the manifest, and restart it before enabling proxy routes. DevFn reports the owning instance and service, leaves the existing profile running, and does not move a lease automatically. Without an active proxy claim, a profile without proxy routes keeps its v0.1 exact, preferred, and stable port behavior.
  - Certificate snapshots: activated explicit certificates are copied into owner-only machine state so an unrelated worktree can stop after the source certificate disappears; replace the source and reactivate the affected route to update it. A failed replacement restores the prior routes with the snapshots they were served with, not the current source files, and reports a failed restore instead of claiming the routes were kept. A replacement killed before the prior teardown loses that rollback copy: the prior lifecycle reports `degraded`, `devfn down` removes this worktree's routes, and the next `up` revalidates the certificate source files.
- Volume deletion, database reset, public tunnels, and other destructive operations are outside ordinary lifecycle commands and require separate explicit tooling and confirmation.

---

<!-- page:docs:reference/testing.md path:/docs/reference/testing -->
# @devfn/testing

> Source package guide for @devfn/testing.


Deterministic fixture manifests, temporary projects, and fake listeners for allocator, lifecycle, crash-recovery, and CLI contract tests.

`@devfn/testing/networking` publishes the networking qualification matrix (`devfn.networking-qualification/v1`) and its harness: fail-closed prerequisite probes, an approval file that names only nonproduction resources and credential variable names, a disposable resource inventory with absence read-back, protected operator state, and receipts that count a scenario as passed only when a live run observed every planned assertion. Fixture tests listed for each scenario are local evidence, never a live pass. An approved Cloudflare tunnel serves one run at a time: a run starts only when no connector is connected to it. See the package README for the `plan`, `run` and `gate` commands.

---

<!-- page:docs:security.md path:/docs/security -->
# Trust and secret handling

> Review manifests, isolate secrets, and confirm public exposure.


Every manifest can declare lifecycle commands. DevFn requires explicit trust for its exact digest before first load and after edits, including JSON manifests. Executable manifests run from a private verified copy and cannot import other files, closing a dependency escape around the digest check.

Runtime children inherit a small base environment plus named `envAllowlist` entries. Sensitive-looking names must also appear in `secretEnv` so effective values are redacted before native logs persist. Credentials are also rejected in resolved literals and command argv, including URL userinfo, `Authorization` headers, credential-named flags, form fields, and JSON keys. These checks are not full secret detection; inspect all manifest literals. Compose services with `secretEnv` use Docker's `none` logging driver. Runtime directories and files default to owner-only modes.

Ports and proxy targets bind to loopback unless the manifest explicitly selects public exposure; `--allow-public` is an additional confirmation on every start. DevFn does not infer a public tunnel. Development domains other than `.localhost` require machine registration that a repository manifest cannot perform, and every selected hostname must resolve only to loopback. DevFn never installs Caddy's internal CA in a trust store. `down` stops only owned instance resources and does not delete persistent volumes. Read the [full security contract](https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions/blob/dev/devfn/docs/content/docs/reference/security.md) before using DevFn with sensitive data.

---
